questions.q: According to the measurement postulate, what values can a measurement of an observable M return?
options: Any real number between 0 and 1
Only one of M's eigenvalues -- never any other number
Always exactly 0 or exactly 1, regardless of what M is
The trace of M
questions.explain: The measurement postulate restricts outcomes to exactly M's eigenvalues -- for Pauli-Z that means only +1 or -1 are ever possible, never any other value.

questions.q: For the Pauli-Z observable, what happens to a qubit's state immediately after a measurement returns the outcome -1?
options: The state remains unchanged in superposition
The state collapses to |1>, the eigenvector of Pauli-Z matching eigenvalue -1
The state becomes the zero vector
The state collapses to |0>, since -1 is a negative number
questions.explain: Pauli-Z's eigenvalue -1 pairs with eigenvector |1> (from Lesson 17), so a measurement outcome of -1 collapses the qubit's state exactly to |1>.

questions.q: For the state |psi> = (3/5)|0> + (4/5)|1>, what is the probability that measuring Pauli-Z returns +1?
options: 1/2, since there are only two possible outcomes
4/5, since that is the amplitude on the other basis state
9/25, since the probability is the squared magnitude of the amplitude on |0>: (3/5)^2 = 9/25
3/5, since that is the amplitude on |0>
questions.explain: The probability of a measurement outcome is the squared magnitude of the amplitude on the matching eigenvector, not the amplitude itself -- (3/5)^2 = 9/25 = 0.36.

questions.q: Why must a Hermitian operator's eigenvalues always be real numbers in the context of quantum measurement?
options: Because eigenvalues are only used for diagonalization, not measurement
Because all matrices have only real eigenvalues
Because Hermitian operators are always diagonal matrices
Because a physical measurement has to produce a real, readable number, not a complex one
questions.explain: Since measurement outcomes must be real, observable-representing matrices are required to be Hermitian specifically because that property guarantees real eigenvalues -- a fact Chapter 5 proves in general.

questions.q: What does 'collapse' mean in the context of quantum measurement?
options: A gradual, reversible fade of the amplitudes back to their original values
The process of normalizing a state vector so its amplitudes sum to 1
The physical destruction of the qubit hardware after a measurement
The irreversible change of the qubit's state from a superposition to exactly the single eigenvector matching the observed eigenvalue
questions.explain: Collapse is the postulate that once a measurement is taken, the pre-measurement superposition is gone and the state becomes exactly the eigenvector corresponding to the observed eigenvalue, with certainty, until acted on again.
